sections.h2: Where to take a deed in Shelby County
sections.html:
Take it to the Shelby County Recorder on the second floor of the county annex at 129 E. Court Street in Sidney. Phone 937-498-7270 or fax 937-498-7272 to reach staff. The counter takes new recordings a quarter hour before the staff stops other business. Monday to Thursday that means a 4:15 p.m. cutoff against a 4:30 p.m. close, and on Fridays 11:45 a.m. against noon. Plan to arrive well ahead of those times.

The Recorder keeps the county's real estate records, which reach back to the county's start, when the land was still part of Miami County. The online index covers July 1, 1989 forward. Older research means a trip to the office, and staff will help, though they do not do genealogy searches for outsiders.

Sidney is the only city in the county. The rest is villages, townships and farmland along the Great Miami River, so a deed here may describe a Sidney street lot, a village house or acreage. The county has 48,230 residents. A farmhouse on a few acres may need a survey or a split approved before it can be deeded separately, so ask the Auditor's office early about description rules.

sections.h2: What does Shelby County charge to record a deed?
sections.html:
Under the 2025 schedule, a deed costs $39 for its first two pages, with $8 for every added page. Most recording fees climbed $5 on January 1, 2025, after Senate Bill 94 added a document preservation surcharge, which ORC 317.32 limits to five dollars.

Shelby County Recorder charges, 2025 schedule

Count the pages before you write the check, because the total moves with each added sheet and each attachment.

sections.h2: What recorder staff look for in a deed
sections.html:
The Recorder's rules are plain:

  • Every document needs a legal description, and it must read as it does on the prior deed. A description with missing parts is rejected.
  • Mail filings need a self-addressed stamped envelope. Without postage for the return, the office holds the document.
  • Marginal notations require the volume and page of the earlier record, and each one adds $4.
  • An affidavit has to say who the current owner of the property is.

The grantor's signature must be acknowledged by an authorized officer, usually a notary, under ORC 5301.01. An unacknowledged deed is not ready for the counter.

The county also posts a public notice on old deed language. Any clause that limits the sale, rental or use of a dwelling by race, color, sex, religion, national origin, handicap or familial status is invalid under federal fair housing law and cannot be enforced, even if it sits in a decades-old recorded deed.

The Shelby County Auditor does, before the Recorder files anything. The real estate transfer fee is $4 per $1,000 of sale price plus $.50 per parcel.

The rate rests on ORC 319.54(G)(3) and the county option in ORC 322.02. The county option falls on the grantor, which makes the seller the usual payer when the deed is delivered.

A few transfers are exempt, among them family gifts, corrective deeds and deeds where no money changes hands. Ask the Auditor before assuming a deal qualifies.

sections.h2: From signing to a recorded deed
sections.html:
There are four steps, in this order. The grantor signs before a notary. The deed goes to the Shelby County Auditor with the transfer fee. The deed then goes to the Recorder, with the recording fee and a stamped return envelope if it travels by mail. Last, the Recorder indexes it, and the new owner's name appears in the county's records.

A title company normally carries a deed through those steps at a closing. A family member handling a transfer alone can do the same in person or by mail. Both offices are in Sidney, so ask each for its current hours before you go, and remember that the Recorder stops taking recordings 15 minutes before it closes.

Once the filing posts, the online index from July 1, 1989 forward lets anyone, including the seller, confirm the deed went on record.

sections.h2: Property tax records and relief programs
sections.html:
The Auditor's real estate section covers valuation and tax rates, revaluation information, owner occupancy and homestead tax reductions, delinquent payment plans and razed or damaged structures. A seller can search a parcel there to see the value on record before listing.

  • A value dispute begins as a Board of Revision complaint. ORC 5715.19 allows filing with the auditor until March 31 of the next year, or until the first-half collection closes if that falls later.
  • The 2026 homestead reduction for seniors and disabled owners is $29,700 of value, with the application filed in the same year by December 31.
  • Back taxes can sometimes be paid through a delinquent payment plan. Ask the Auditor for terms.

At closing the title agent requests the tax payoff from the county. Because Ohio bills real estate in two halves, the amount owed depends on when in the year the sale closes.

sections.h2: Selling a house that needs work
sections.html:
Many Shelby County houses are older village homes or farmhouses, and some need repairs a lender would balk at. A sale to a cash buyer is one route. The deed process described above is the same either way: signature before a notary, the Auditor's transfer fee, then the Recorder.

If the house came to you through a family estate, gather the recorded deed, any affidavit that names the current owner, and the death or probate paperwork your title company asks for. The Recorder will only file what is complete and acknowledged, so a missing signature or notary stamp costs you a second trip. For a mailed filing, add the stamped return envelope and a check for the exact fee. A cash buyer or title company usually handles these details, but it helps to know what they are doing on your behalf.

Before you sign a contract, check three things. Confirm the legal description on your current deed is complete, since a description with missing parts is rejected. Ask the Auditor whether the transfer qualifies for an exemption. And find out whether any back taxes need a payoff at closing, so the title agent is not surprised.

faqs.q: What are the Shelby County Recorder's hours for recording a deed?
faqs.a: New recordings are accepted until 4:15 p.m. Monday to Thursday and until 11:45 a.m. Friday. Other office business continues 15 minutes longer each day.

faqs.q: How much is the Shelby County recording fee for a two-page deed?
faqs.a: It is $39 on the 2025 schedule, which covers the first two pages. Pages beyond that cost $8 each, a non-standard document adds $20, and each marginal notation adds $4.

faqs.q: Will the Recorder hold my deed if I mail it?
faqs.a: Yes, if you leave out the return envelope. Mailed documents need a stamped, self-addressed envelope, and without one the office holds the paper instead of mailing it back.

faqs.q: What is the Shelby County conveyance fee?
faqs.a: The real estate transfer fee is $4 per $1,000 of sale price plus fifty cents for each parcel. It is paid at the Auditor's office, ahead of recording.

faqs.q: Can I search Shelby County deeds from home?
faqs.a: Partly. The Recorder's website carries an index from July 1, 1989 forward. Earlier books stay at the office, where staff help visitors search but do not take genealogy requests.
